newsitem.title: GREECE: Greenpeace blocks oil refinery in Greece.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace blocks oil refinery in Greece.

text.p: Greenpeace activists on Tuesday chained themselves around the docking facilities of the Motor Oil refinery port and accused the oil industry of polluting the environment.
Two ships were prevented from leaving the refinery near the Corinth canal by four activists who chained themselves to their mooring buoys. Another two activists were chained to loading cranes.
The refinery, jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Vardinoyannis group, is the biggest in Greece and handles about five million tonnes of fuel annually.
Greenpeace speedboats prevented tankers from trying to dock and the environmental group's ship Arctic Sunrise helped block access to the port.
"We demand that Motor Oil and the oil industry are held accountable for polluting the environment," Greenpeace activist Nikos Charalambides told Reuters aboard the Arctic Sunrise.
He said Greenpeace would abandon the blockade only if a list of conditions sent to the ministries of merchant marine and environment were satisfied.
"We will stay until our demands are met. If it takes hours, days or weeks, that's OK. We are patient," he added.
Greenpeace says a major oil spill at the refinery in August was the last straw in a long series of mishaps.
It wants the government to make stricter laws on oil pollution, ban the use of chemical dispersants and prohibit loading at refineries at night or during bad weather.
A large but still unspecified quantity of oil leaked when a lightning bolt struck a worker as a Motor Oil-owned tanker was loading at the facility at night and during a storm.
Greenpeace claims that loading at night without oil booms is a recipe for disaster and that the refinery ignored a weather service warning that a storm was coming.

Motor Oil officials deny knowledge of a weather warning and say they cleaned up after the freak accident despite the fact that according to Greek law, the ship was responsible for the accident. A legal inquiry into the spill has not been completed.

"On our own initiative we apply more safety measures than required by law. If the law wants more, we will comply but we already have more than the standard," Constantine Vassilakis, a Motor Oil representative, said at a meeting with Greenpeace.
He did not deny that the refinery reports between six and 17 oil spills a year but said they were tiny and that Motor Oil should not be penalised for being honest in reporting them.
"I demand that Greenpeace leaves immediately. They are risking the safety of this refinery which has not been designed to deal with lunatics," Vassilakis said.

Government and port authority officials, as well as an assistant public prosecutor, also participated in the meeting aimed at defusing tensions but there was no official reaction to Greenpeace's demands.

Aramco bought a 50 percent stake in the Vardinoyannis family's Motor Oil Corinth Refineries SA and the accompanying Avinoil Industries distribution network in Greece for $379 million earlier this year. Motor Oil employs about 1,300 people and had a 1994 turnover of about $750 million.
